**Description**

```
For more than a thousand years, Cham kings ruled parts of the coast of today's central Vietnam. Champa ended as a state in 1832 — but the Cham people, their towers, gods and festivals are still here.
Sources: M. Vickery, Champa Revised (2005); W. Southworth, 'Champa', Oxford Handbook of Early Southeast Asia (2022); A. Hardy et al., Champa: Territories and Networks (EFEO 2019); J. Whitmore and others in The Cham of Vietnam (2011); G. Wade, The Ming shi Account of Champa (2003); N. Weber, JSEAS 43(1) 2012; Po Dharma; Ho Ping-ti (1956) and Sweeney et al. (2011) on Champa rice; Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư; UNESCO (My Son Sanctuary; Art of pottery-making of Chăm people); GSO Vietnam 2019 Census.
Casualty figures for 1471 differ between the Vietnamese chronicle and Ming records; we give both. Illustrations and narration are AI-assisted.
Corrections welcome in the comments.
```
